transcript.text: Hi Tanvi, good to meet you. I'd like to spend the next 15 minutes or so going through your resume and the stories behind it, and I'll leave time for your questions at the end. What finance skill have you picked up recently in your course?
transcript.why: This was a warm-up question to help you settle in. It isn't part of the feedback.

transcript.text: Hi sir, great to meet you as well so actually I think the most recent finance skill that I have picked up at IIM Lucknow is building LBO models, like earlier I knew basic valuation from undergrad and a bit from my CFA Level 1 prep but at IIML in this first year we had this investment banking workshop where I learned to structure full LBOs with different tranches of debt and sensitivity to entry and exit multiples so um one assignment I did was for an actual pharma company and I modelled out the sources and uses, and also built the cash flow waterfall just to analyse if the private equity firm could meet its target IRR and I think working with real India-specific cost of debt assumptions and covenants was something I’d never done before so I feel I’ve become much more confident now about LBOs beyond just reading about them in books
Thanks. Walk me through your background: your studies and the experiences that led you to pursue finance.
transcript.why: Your answer gave a brief example of a finance skill you recently developed, so I moved on to your broader background.

transcript.text: sure sir so actually I’ve always been a numbers person so in school I took up commerce with maths and then at St Xavier’s I did my BCom Hons and there I was part of the finance society from my first year so we did company valuations and some competitions uh but the real turning point was my internship at EY during undergrad where I worked on transaction diligence for an FMCG distributor so I was analysing their accounts and flagged four crore of one-time credits that weren’t coming from normal operations and the lead there really appreciated my attention to detail so that was a kind of confidence boost then in my final year I got to head the Rotaract club as president where we raised funds for a library project that made me realise I enjoy working with money in a way that creates social as well as financial value and after clearing CFA Level 1 I realised I wanted to go deeper into finance so that’s why I went for IIM Lucknow and focused on finance electives and I also joined the student-run investment fund at the Finance Club where I got hands-on exposure to managing a portfolio so all these experiences sort of confirmed that I really want a finance career, ideally investment banking or buy-side in the long term
At Kotak, you built a valuation model for a hospital chain's QIP. What were you trying to solve for the client?

so um in that project the hospital chain wanted to raise capital through a Qualified Institutional Placement, basically QIP, and our mandate at Kotak was to advise them on the equity pricing and how much capital they could realistically raise without too much dilution so my role was to build out both a DCF and a trading comps model and for the DCF I had to project their cash flows, like occupancy rates and ARPOB, average revenue per occupied bed, were the two key drivers so I worked closely with one of our VPs to get realistic assumptions on those and then for the trading comps I benchmarked them against nine listed hospital players you know like Apollo, Narayana and so on and the main challenge was that our client’s margins had just improved so I had to justify if a premium to peers made sense and also run sensitivity to see, for example, if occupancy goes down by 2-3 percentage points what’s the effect on the valuation so in the end what I presented to the client CFO was not just a single fair value but a scenario range reflecting the upside and downside and that helped them decide the floor price for the QIP so overall the client appreciated how actionable the output was especially because we linked the model directly to public comps and real operating parameters
What made you choose both DCF and trading comps for this QIP analysis?
transcript.why: You explained how you built both models and used them in the pricing discussion, but not why those approaches were appropriate for this mandate. I asked about the valuation choice.

transcript.text: so actually sir I chose to do both DCF and trading comps because they sort of complement each other and give a more complete picture especially in a QIP situation, like with DCF I could really capture the hospital chain’s specific cash flow growth story, because they had plans for bed expansion and their margins were trending up so DCF let us capture value from those projections but at the same time trading comps are really important for market validation since institutional investors in a QIP will definitely benchmark the issue price against peers so if we only gave a DCF, we’d risk being out of line with market sentiment say if the sector is trading at 22 times EBIT and our DCF implied like 30 times, then it needs to be justified so by running both and showing the CFO how our intrinsic valuation compared with current multiples, we could recommend a range based on both fundamentals and market reality and that really helped build confidence in our pricing proposal and also gave the client flexibility during investor discussions
Let's move to the student-managed fund. As Finance Club coordinator, you ran the fund with INR 25 lakh. How did you decide where to deploy its capital?
transcript.why: Your answer explained why you combined the two valuation approaches and how the comparison supported the pricing recommendation, so I moved to another finance decision.

transcript.text: yeah so actually at the Finance Club we run this student-managed fund which is like a live equity portfolio and I was the coordinator last year so the core approach we took was a mix of bottom-up stock picking and some macro overlay basically first we did a sector allocation exercise at the start of the year looking at macro trends you know things like RBI rate direction, earnings cycle, sector rotations and after some discussions with the seniors and faculty advisor we set target weights for sectors like banking, pharma, FMCG and IT but the main alpha we went after was with bottom-up fundamental picks so every stock idea went through a four-member investment committee, I myself pitched a specialty chemicals stock last August for example where I wrote an equity research note modelling their expected margin expansion post-capex and peer comps and we agreed to initiate with a 5 percent portfolio allocation for it, just to keep risk in check so we used a strict position sizing framework not more than 8 percent for a single stock and for risk management we had stop-losses and a quarterly review for calls that underperform benchmarks so over the year it was pretty structured, I’d say we met monthly to revalidate our thesis and actually exited one IT stock after an earnings miss and reallocated to PSU banks when we saw valuation comfort so our decision making was very research-driven and quite collaborative actually, and that played a role in helping us beat the Nifty by like 2.4 percent for the year
You mentioned the fund beat the Nifty by 2.4%. How exactly was that return calculated and compared with the Nifty 50 over FY26?
transcript.why: You described the fund's performance as 14.2% versus 11.8% for the Nifty 50, so I asked how those figures were calculated and compared over the year.

transcript.text: right so basically for calculating the fund returns we took the starting corpus which was twenty-five lakh at the beginning of FY26, and then tracked all inflows and outflows including dividends and any cash we parked temporarily and at the end of the year we took the closing value including mark-to-market for all holdings so the absolute return was just total gain divided by starting corpus um but to make it directly comparable with the Nifty 50 we used a time-weighted return because sometimes we had interim cash like from stock exits before reallocating so time-weighting helped us strip out those effects and just focus on our stock selection alpha and for benchmarking, every month we checked our portfolio’s value progression versus what would have happened if the same corpus was invested in the Nifty ETF so we compounded those monthly Nifty returns to get the same period’s index growth so over the full year our fund delivered 14.2 percent and the Nifty was at 11.8 percent so that’s how we got the outperformance number, and we also did a risk-adjusted check using standard deviation just to make sure it wasn’t coming from higher portfolio volatility
Let's turn to the CFA Research Challenge. You initiated coverage on a cement company with a SELL call. What drove your recommendation?
transcript.why: Your answer explained how the fund return was calculated and compared with the Nifty 50, including how interim cash was handled.

transcript.text: yeah so this was actually a really interesting challenge for us so the company we covered was a mid-cap cement producer with most of its plants in East India and when we started building the model, the street was quite bullish because there was talk of infra push and rural housing but when I dug into their numbers I found a couple of red flags um first, their capacity utilisation was already around 85 percent so future volume growth would need heavy capex, and from management calls we learnt they didn’t have clear timelines or funding plans for new lines so I baked in more moderate volume growth than consensus and on the realisations side, they were facing a lot of pricing pressure especially from bigger pan-India players entering that region, so our blended realisation assumption was lower than most other research reports and also their power and fuel costs were spiking because they rely a lot on petcoke and diesel so EBITDA margins were coming down year-on-year so when I ran the DCF and the multiples, the stock was trading at around 15 times forward EV/EBITDA while our target justified maybe 11 to 12 times, so there was about 20 percent downside to the current price and when we stress-tested it for higher input costs or lower price hikes the downside scenarios grew even more so our final pitch was a SELL call mainly based on stretched valuation, higher opex risk, and an overoptimistic consensus on new project ramp-up and that’s actually what the judges appreciated, that we didn’t just go with the street view and had proper backing for a contrarian call
Which decisions or pieces of analysis in that recommendation did you personally own?
transcript.why: Your answer explained the team's thesis and the evidence behind the SELL call, but your own responsibilities were not fully distinct. I asked which decisions and analysis were personally yours.

transcript.text: so yeah I actually owned a few of the core parts of the analysis myself, for example I was the main person responsible for the demand and realisation forecast so I built the operating model bottom-up, spoke to a couple of industry channel partners through LinkedIn to get feedback on cement pricing trends in East India, and I also led the sensitivity analysis on power and fuel costs because that was a key margin driver that year um I worked directly on the DCF part as well, setting up the projections for revenue, capex and working capital and I validated our terminal growth and discount rate assumptions by benchmarking with other listed cements and Bloomberg estimates so, basically, my work formed the backbone of the financial projections and valuation, and I also wrote the investment thesis section in our report which summarised the main reasons for downside and laid out the bear and base case scenarios so I’d say the analysis I did personally was both on the numbers side and the story we told in the final presentation
Let’s move to your EY internship. What did you have to figure out first when you normalised EBITDA for the FMCG distributor?

recent_exchanges.candidate: so for that particular credit I used both quantitative and qualitative baselines to confirm it was a one-time adjustment so first I looked at the past three years of their vendor credit line items on a month-wise basis and saw that credits of that size just didn’t appear in any previous year or month it was a sudden spike in the P&L and when I asked the finance manager, he explained it was basically compensation from a FMCG principal whose product line was being discontinued and replaced so I got a copy of the agreement as well just to be sure and found it was a non-recurring payout, actually noted as such in the schedule so my baseline was what the vendor credits looked like in normal years—usually it was a few lakhs in discount settlements versus this four crore lump sum only in that quarter so aligning with standard diligence practice, I followed the recurring run-rate from prior years and the accounting policy for such non-operating receipts and got a sign-off from the EY engagement manager so that gave me confidence it should be treated as a one-off and taken out for a fair normalised EBITDA

recent_exchanges.interviewer: Thanks, Tanvi. That’s everything from my side. What questions do you have for me?
recent_exchanges.candidate: thank you sir um I actually had two quick questions if that’s alright so first, I’d love to know from your experience what you think sets apart a really strong analyst or associate in your team, especially in the first year like what are the specific skills or work habits you’ve seen make the most difference and second, could you share a bit about how the firm approaches training and mentorship for new joiners is it more structured, like formal programs, or does it happen more through live deals and working closely with seniors

recent_exchanges.interviewer: I’d rather not guess about the team’s specific expectations or training structure. The hiring team can share how mentorship and live-deal learning work there. Is there anything else you’d like to know?
